extracted.intended_audience: writers, critics, and students of rhetoric/poetics interested in achieving or judging the Sublime in prose and poetry
extracted.subtask_description: A practical/theoretical guide to producing and recognising the Sublime in literature: lists principal sources (grandeur of thought, passions, figures, diction, structure), faults to avoid, and tests for true vs. false sublimity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Command of language (preliminary gift)
rubrics_metrics.description: The preliminary gift on which the five sources of sublimity depend: an assured control over language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Longinus explicitly treats Command of language as the necessary prerequisite for sublimity (section VIII). Without a firm command of words and expression, the other sources (thought, passions, figures, diction, structure) cannot produce the Sublime.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grandeur of thought
rubrics_metrics.description: Grandeur or loftiness of conception is the most important source of sublimity: a lofty cast of mind produces sublime thoughts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listed as the first and most important source (VIII, IX). Examples: Homeric images that measure by the extent of the world; lofty, simple thoughts (e.g., the silence of Ajax) that are admirable for sheer force. Guidance: cultivate generous, aspiring thoughts — 'true eloquence can be found only in those whose spirit is generous and aspiring.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Vigorous and spirited treatment of the passions
rubrics_metrics.description: A powerful, appropriate display of passion (the Pathetic) contributes to sublimity when genuine and well-timed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listed as the second principal source (VIII). Longinus warns that not all passions are lofty (pity, grief, fear may be low), but 'nothing is so conducive to sublimity as an appropriate display of genuine passion, which bursts out with a kind of "fine madness" and divine inspiration.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Artifice in the employment of figures (figures of thought and speech)
rubrics_metrics.description: Skillful use of rhetorical figures — both figures of thought and of speech — can produce sublimity when employed with art and restraint.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listed as the third source (VIII). Longinus treats figures as an artful adjunct that can assist sublimity but also warns of dangers (excessive novelty, risky transitions, hyperboles, plural-for-singular usages) that may lead to faults.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dignified expression: choice of words and metaphors
rubrics_metrics.description: A dignified, appropriate diction — right word choice and metaphors — is a core source of sublime style.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listed as the fourth source (VIII, subdivided into (a) proper choice of words and (b) use of metaphors and ornaments). Longinus values 'appropriate and striking words' and cautions against mere 'word-tasting' or obsession with 'colour' of words; 'Beautiful words are the very light of thought.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Majesty and elevation of structure
rubrics_metrics.description: High, elevated structural arrangement of a passage or work (majesty of composition) is a source of sublimity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listed as the fifth source (VIII). Includes elevation of overall architecture, climaxing, and the welding of striking incidents into an animate whole; structure can be an artful means to sustain sublime effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection and combination of striking circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: Choosing the most striking, pertinent incidents and combining them into a unified, animate whole attracts the reader and produces sublimity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Section X: example of Sappho — felicity lies in 'the felicity with which she chooses and unites together the most striking and powerful features.' Guidance: select striking circumstances actually observed or appropriate, then fuse them with skill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conviction and selection as essential merits
rubrics_metrics.description: Conviction (moral/intellectual force) and the power of selection (choosing what to keep and what to omit) are essential qualities of high literature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From the introduction: 'He proclaims the essential merits of conviction, and of selection.' Longinus emphasizes these as central to dignity and force of style; selection ties to avoiding tediousness and selecting only what contributes to sublimity.

rubrics_metrics.name: True Sublimity: sustained, pregnant, and universally moving effect
rubrics_metrics.description: True sublimity sustains beyond immediate reading, is 'pregnant in suggestion', hard to distract from, takes strong hold on memory, and pleases across varied readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion for distinguishing true vs. specious sublimity (VII): 'When a passage is pregnant in suggestion... takes a strong and lasting hold on the memory... we may be sure that we have lighted on the true Sublime.' Conversely, if 'the longer you read it, the less you think of it,' it is not truly sublime.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of bombast and grandiloquence
rubrics_metrics.description: Bombast (hollow, affected bulk and overblown phrases) is a vice that exceeds and corrupts the Sublime.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Longinus warns bombast is 'one of the hardest things to avoid' (III). Examples: exaggerated compounds like 'curling torrent flame', 'vomiting to heaven', and overwrought conceits; such phrases move from tragic to burlesque and produce confusion rather than energy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of puerility, frigidity, and false sentiment
rubrics_metrics.description: Puerility (pedantic over-elaboration), frigidity (coldness of style), and false sentiment (ill-timed or empty emotion) are severe vices that degrade writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defined in III–IV: puerility = 'a pedantic habit of mind' leading to paltriness and silliness; false sentiment = 'an ill-timed and empty display of emotion' unconnected to subject; frigidity = striking absurdities, childish conceits or cold, awkward expressions even in otherwise able writers. Longinus gives many examples (Amphicrates, Tirnaeus, Xenophon lapses).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection of novelty-for-novelty's-sake
rubrics_metrics.description: Pursuing novelty in thought or expression merely to be different leads to grotesque improprieties and ruins taste.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Longinus traces many stylistic improprieties to 'the pursuit of novelty in thought' (section IV–V), observing that ornaments of style that secure success may also be sources of failure if novelty is pursued without judgment. Guidance: avoid strange conceits that sacrifice correctness and dignity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art can train but must not suffocate genius
rubrics_metrics.description: Technical instruction and method can teach aspects of sublimity (precision, timing, restraint), but art must allow the genius to abandon himself to inspiration where needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In II Longinus argues against the view that the Sublime is purely inborn: 'to determine the right degree and the right moment... is the peculiar province of scientific method.' Yet he qualifies: 'a writer can only learn from art when he is to abandon himself to the direction of his genius.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Dignity and fire of style derive from dignity and fire of soul
rubrics_metrics.description: The external features of style (dignity, fire) reflect an internal moral/intellectual greatness — the soul of the writer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From the introduction: 'He traces dignity and fire of style to dignity and fire of soul.' Longinus treats literary greatness as rooted in moral and intellectual greatness; therefore cultivation of the mind/soul is part of producing sublime writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical treatises must define subject and show methods
rubrics_metrics.description: A useful technical treatise should (1) define the subject and (2) indicate how and by what methods a reader may master it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critique of Caecilius (early pages): Caecilius fails because he 'passes by as immaterial the question how we might be able to exalt our own genius' — Longinus insists a proper manual must both define and give methods/practice.
